title: Nucleation and Enhancement of Superconductivity under Tip-Induced Strain Fields
authors: Ghulam Mohmad, Vishal Tripathi, Goutam Sheet
abstract: A metallic point contact formed on a non-superconducting or weakly superconducting material often nucleates or enhances superconductivity confined under the contact. However, no unified theoretical description of the phenomenon exists. We show that the spatially inhomogeneous, predominantly uniaxial nature of the stress field under a point contact is fundamental for such tip-induced and tip-enhanced superconductivity (TISC/TESC). We also show that the coupling of such a stress field to the electronic structure can be estimated through an experimentally measurable uniaxial coupling scale $C^{\mathrm{exp}}$. Combining Hertzian contact mechanics with a Ginzburg-Landau variational analysis, we derive a criterion for the nucleation of TISC/TESC and determine $C^{\mathrm{exp}}$ for twenty-one materials. For topological semimetals with ungapped band crossings, the framework explains observed critical temperatures with no free parameters and for all others, $C^{\mathrm{exp}}$ provides a direct experimental determination of the uniaxial strain sensitivity and a target scale for microscopic theories.The work predicts TISC in elemental Sb and Y with $T_c \approx 2.8$\,K and $T_c \approx 12$\,K respectively.
summary: This paper develops a unified theory explaining how localized stress fields from point contacts can induce or enhance superconductivity. By merging Hertzian contact mechanics with Ginzburg-Landau analysis, the authors derive a quantitative nucleation criterion dependent on an experimentally measurable uniaxial coupling scale ($C^{\mathrm{exp}}$). This framework successfully predicts superconducting behavior in various materials, including elemental Sb and Y.
main_problem: The lack of a unified theoretical description for superconductivity nucleation or enhancement induced by localized, inhomogeneous strain fields generated under metallic point contacts.
main_result: A quantitative criterion derived from combining Hertzian contact mechanics and Ginzburg-Landau theory establishes the necessary conditions for tip-induced superconductivity (TISC/TESC). The framework successfully predicts critical temperatures for elemental Sb and Y.
method: The authors combine continuum mechanics (Hertzian theory) to model strain fields with a variational analysis of the Ginzburg-Landau free energy functional to determine the superconducting order parameter's stability.
model_or_system: The system involves a metallic tip creating a spatially inhomogeneous, predominantly uniaxial stress field ($\sigma_{zz}$) on a superconductor. The theoretical framework models superconductivity nucleation by solving for bound states in an effective potential well derived from the strain coupling to the electronic structure.
key_observables: Critical temperature enhancement ($\Delta T_c$), the experimentally measurable uniaxial coupling scale ($C^{\mathrm{exp}}$), and the superconducting order parameter $\psi(r)$.
important_parameters: The uniaxial coupling scale $C^{\mathrm{exp}}$, the contact radius ($a$), maximum pressure ($p_{max}$), and the dimensionless local enhancement strength ($s_0$).
main_assumptions: The stress field is predominantly uniaxial, allowing for a simplified strain-coupling model. The analysis relies on approximating the complex physics using Ginzburg-Landau theory coupled with Hertzian contact mechanics.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares theoretical and measured profiles of pressure/strain; Figure 2 uses the Rayleigh-Ritz functional to define the nucleation threshold ($Q=0$); Figure 3 plots calculated nucleation criteria across different material regimes.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical necessity of uniaxial strain for TISC/TESC. It then develops a quantitative criterion using GL theory and contact mechanics, classifying materials based on how $C^{\mathrm{exp}}$ relates to theoretical coupling scales ($C_{th}$ vs $C_{vol}$). Finally, it applies this framework to predict specific material outcomes.
why_interesting: The work provides a highly structured, predictive theoretical framework linking macroscopic mechanical measurements (contact pressure) directly to microscopic quantum phenomena (superconductivity), which is valuable for understanding strain-mediated quantum effects in condensed matter systems.
